name: React
role: Frontend developers use React to compose interactive interfaces from reusable components.
technical: Components express output from props and state. Events update state; the UI is rendered again. Routing and application-level data access require additional choices.
tradeoffs: Keep state ownership explicit, use stable list keys and test keyboard behavior. Rendering a login screen does not implement server authorization.
exercise: Build a searchable list with loading, empty and error states.

name: Angular
role: Application teams use Angular for structured browser applications with integrated platform features.
technical: Components, templates, dependency injection and routing organize application behavior. TypeScript supports typed interfaces; reactive state helps update views.
tradeoffs: Keep service boundaries clear and avoid turning every component into a global-state consumer. Budget browser bundles and test form accessibility.
exercise: Build a routed settings page with validation and an unsaved-changes state.

name: Vue.js
role: Frontend developers use Vue for incremental enhancement or complete component-based applications.
technical: Declarative templates and reactive state connect data to rendered UI. Single-file components can colocate template, behavior and styling.
tradeoffs: Distinguish derived state from side effects. Choose routing, server rendering and data-fetching approaches to match the application.
exercise: Create a filterable catalogue with reusable item components.

name: Next.js
role: Web application teams use Next.js to combine React interfaces with routing and server-side application features.
technical: Server and client components divide work between environments. Rendering, data fetching and caching choices affect what ships to the browser.
tradeoffs: Understand cache invalidation and the server/client boundary. Authenticate and authorize server operations; do not expose secrets through client bundles.
exercise: Build a read-only documentation route and compare static and request-time rendering.

name: Node.js
role: Backend and tooling developers use Node.js to run JavaScript outside a browser. It is a runtime, not a UI or application framework.
technical: The runtime supplies server APIs and asynchronous I/O. An event loop coordinates callbacks and tasks; CPU-heavy work can delay other requests.
tradeoffs: Bound request sizes, use timeouts and move expensive work off the event loop where appropriate. A framework adds routing conventions above the runtime.
exercise: Create a small HTTP endpoint with explicit error responses.

name: Express
role: Node.js backend developers use Express for HTTP routing and middleware pipelines.
technical: Requests pass through configured middleware and route handlers. The framework provides HTTP conveniences without prescribing an entire data architecture.
tradeoffs: Middleware order matters. Validate input, centralize error responses and configure proxy trust deliberately for the actual deployment.
exercise: Build an API with validation, a not-found response and an error handler.

name: Django
role: Backend developers use Django for data-driven sites with models, routing, templates and administration.
technical: An object-relational mapper maps models to database operations. URL routing selects views; templates render output and migrations evolve schema.
tradeoffs: Enforce authorization at the view and object level. Review query counts, migration behavior and deployment settings; an admin interface is not a public API.
exercise: Build a reading list with ownership checks and database constraints.

name: FastAPI
role: API developers use FastAPI for typed request contracts and generated API documentation.
technical: Python annotations describe inputs and outputs. Validation and OpenAPI generation support explicit contracts; async endpoints can cooperate during I/O waits.
tradeoffs: A validated shape is not permission to act. Separate validation, authentication and authorization; avoid blocking calls inside async request paths.
exercise: Build a paginated API that validates limits and tests error payloads.

name: Laravel
role: PHP application teams use Laravel for web products with common routing, database and application-service needs.
technical: Routing, dependency injection, Eloquent models, migrations and queues provide conventions around application work.
tradeoffs: Use policies for authorization and validate input. Make background jobs idempotent and consider transactions before sending follow-up work.
exercise: Build a request workflow with a policy check and queued notification.

name: Ruby on Rails
role: Product developers use Rails to build database-backed web applications around shared conventions.
technical: MVC separates models, views and controllers. Active Record and migrations organize relational persistence; routing connects requests to actions.
tradeoffs: Keep authorization explicit and watch query volume. Use transactions and constraints for durable invariants rather than relying only on form validation.
exercise: Build a small issue tracker with per-user access and model tests.

name: Astro
role: Documentation and content-site developers use Astro to deliver pages with selective interactivity.
technical: Islands architecture isolates interactive components while keeping the rest of the page focused on HTML. Rendering and deployment choices depend on the project.
tradeoffs: Only hydrate components that need client behavior. Check content provenance, accessible navigation and the cost of third-party scripts.
exercise: Build a documentation site with one interactive search component.

name: WordPress
role: Publishers, site administrators and developers use WordPress to manage content and extend sites through themes and plugins.
technical: The CMS supplies content workflows and extension points. Themes present content; plugins add functionality and may expand the application’s trust boundary.
tradeoffs: Review plugin maintenance, user capabilities, updates and backups. Editorial access and administrative access should be distinct.
exercise: Model an editorial workflow with separate author and administrator capabilities.
